chunks.arabic_text: مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ بْنِ شَمُّونَ، أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ، أَصْلُهُ بَصْرِيٌّ. وَاقِفٌ، ثُمَّ غَلَا، ضَعِيفٌ، مُتَهَافِتٌ، لَا يُلْتَفَتُ إِلَيْهِ، وَلَا إِلَى مُصَنَّفَاتِهِ، وَسَائِرُ مَا يُنْسَبُ إِلَيْهِ.

translations.en: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun, Abu Ja'far, his origin was Basran. A wāqifī, then he became a ghālī. Weak, collapsed, he is not turned to nor is his writings and the rest of what is attributed to him.

en.summary: This entry from al-Ghadā'irī’s *Kitab al-Du'afā* characterizes Muḥammad ibn al--Ḥasan ibn Shammūn as a Basran narrator who transitioned from the *Wāqifiyya* sect (who held that Imam al-Kāẓim was the final Imam) to the *Ghulāt* (superiors), ultimately being deemed weak and unreliable. His classification highlights the critical Shia methodology of tracking sectarian shifts in narrators, as his move from a specific doctrinal stance to exaggeration (*ghuluw*) rendered his hadiths less authoritative for juristic derivation.
en.seo_question: Who is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shammun and what is his status in Shia hadith sciences?

key_terms.وَاقِفٌ: A follower who stops at one Imam (usually Ali or Muhammad al-Baqir) and does not accept subsequent Imams
key_terms.غَلَا: To exceed bounds, often referring to Ghawls who attribute divine qualities to Imams
key_terms.ضَعِيفٌ: Weak, referring to a narrator with less than perfect reliability
key_terms.مُتَهَافِتٌ: Collapsed or fallen, indicating a decline in status or reliability
